locator: §3.1, 'The quasi-realist is someone who endorses an anti-realist metaphysical stance but who seeks, through philosophical maneuvering, to earn the right for moral discourse to enjoy all the trappings of realist talk.' With: 'If the quasi-realist program succeeds in vindicating the use of the truth predicate for moral sentences, and if in addition it makes it permissible to say “It is a fact that stealing is wrong,” “It is a mind-independent fact that stealing is wrong,” “Stealing would be wrong even if our attitude toward it were different,” and so on—mimicking all and any of the moral realist’s assertions—then in what sense is quasi-realism quasi-realism?'
interpretation: Blackburn's quasi-realist program (Blackburn 1984, 1993, 1998), as the entry reports it. Read as: the program aims to earn the right to all realist talk, and the entry names the mind-independence counterfactual among that talk. Only the aim is recorded. The second sentence is conditional: the entry does not say the program succeeds, and it raises exactly here the collapse challenge (Wright 1988, Dreier 2018) that MIMIC-THEORY-COLLAPSES formalizes. The entry presents quasi-realism as a noncognitivist program while noting that Blackburn calls his view 'projectivism' (Blackburn 1996). Attribution reading on a secondary witness: the claim records the position the entry reports, not a thesis of the entry's author. No primary text is pinnable (in copyright, no immutable open text).
